judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is a link in the article's Language panel whose text is the language's name written in that language ("🇮🇱 עברית"). In the snapshot and in the live page's HTML, neither the <a> nor its <span> has a lang attribute, and the only lang on the page is lang="en" on <html>, so the text is announced with English pronunciation rules. The Understanding document for 3.1.2 describes exactly this case (alternative-language links whose text is the language's name in that language, each marked with lang) as how the criterion is met, and H58 is the sufficient technique. The panel is collapsed by default (the links have tabindex=-1), but they are exposed in the accessibility tree and shown when the panel opens, so they are content of the page. The proper-name and single-word exceptions do not apply: the change of language is intended. A real failure of 3.1.2.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The newsletter sign-up field (placeholder "Enter your email", type="email") asks for the user's own email address, one of the purposes listed in WCAG 2.2 section 7. The snapshot and the live HTML show no autocomplete attribute, and type="email" only gives the data format, not that the field is the user's own email. Nothing else exposes the purpose programmatically, so H98 is not met and the field fails 1.3.5. (It also has no label other than its placeholder, a separate 3.3.2/4.1.2 issue.)

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: "Medical professionals" is a link in the Halloween-themed audience banner at the top of the page (class AudienceBanner_audience-nav-halloween, still present on the live page). Its CSS colour is #6f6f8c; I measured the screenshot pixels behind it myself: the background is a peach gradient around #e7d6cd to #ecddd5, giving about 3.54 to 3.67:1. The text is 14 px at weight 500, which is not large text, so 4.5:1 is required. A real failure of 1.4.3.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The h3 "Mr Alex Day" is the title of an image card. In the screenshot it sits directly above a large photo of Mr Alex Day (alt text: "Mr Alex Day, Consultant Ophthalmologist...") with a "View larger" control, and the paragraphs just before introduce him as the surgeon quoted in the article. The heading names exactly what the card under it shows, so it describes its content and meets 2.4.6. Whether a heading is the right markup for an image caption is a 1.3.1 question, not a 2.4.6 failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The inline link "setting off fireworks" sits in the sentence "For years, we've followed the tradition of setting off fireworks and going to..." and leads to the site's article "Managing PTSD during fireworks season". It is an editorial cross-reference: the text and the destination are about the same topic (fireworks), and with the sentence as context a user can tell it leads to related reading about fireworks. 2.4.4 does not require link text to match or summarise the destination's title. None of its documented failures (F63, F84, F89) applies, and the link is not ambiguous or misleading enough to stop someone deciding whether to follow it. The finding applies a stricter text-must-match-title rule than the criterion.
